since we assume supθ‖m⁡(w,y,θ)‖2≤D\sup_{\theta}\|m(w,y;\theta)\|_{2}\leq D for all w,yw,y and ‖α^−α0‖L2​(Ps)=oℙ​(1)\|\widehat{\alpha}-\alpha_{0}\|_{L^{2}(P^{s})}=o_{\mathbb{P}}(1) by nuisance consistency. This completes the proof of consistency. ∎

Appendix D Details on Riesz Losses

In this section, we discuss the Riesz loss outlined in Equation (4). Introduced in Chernozhukov et al. (2022b) and later in expanded upon in Chernozhukov et al. (2022a); Chernozhukov et al. (2023), Riesz losses provide a principled approach rooted in empirical risk minimization framework for estimating complicated nuisances.

In this appendix, we specifically consider the problem of estimating the nuisance function α0​(w,c):=c​ω0​(w)π0​(w)\alpha_{0}(w,c):=c\frac{\omega_{0}(w)}{\pi_{0}(w)}, where ω0\omega_{0} and π0\pi_{0} are as outlined in Section 3. The naive approach for estimating α0\alpha_{0} would be to construct ML estimators for ω0\omega_{0} and π0\pi_{0}, say by using the predicted probabilities associated with a classifier. The issue with this naive “plug-in” approach is twofold. First, a high-quality classifier for predicting non-compliance or source/target membership will not necessarily yield consistent conditional probability estimates. Second, since α0\alpha_{0} depends on the ratio between ω0\omega_{0} and π0\pi_{0}, any errors in nuisance estimation will compound multiplicatively.

Instead of constructing plug-in estimates, we can directly learn α0\alpha_{0} via loss minimization. The following proposition shows that the Riesz loss outlined in Equation (4) directly specifies as its minimizer β0​(w):=ω0​(w)π0​(w)\beta_{0}(w):=\frac{\omega_{0}(w)}{\pi_{0}(w)}.

Proposition D.1.

The function β0​(w)\beta_{0}(w) satisfies:

β0=argminβ:𝒲→ℝ{𝔼s[C⋅β(W)2]−2𝔼t[β(W)]},\beta_{0}=\arg\min_{\beta:\mathcal{W}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}}\left\{\mathbb{E}_{s}[C\cdot\beta(W)^{2}]-2\mathbb{E}_{t}[\beta(W)]\right\},

where the argument minimizer is taken over all measurable functions of WW.

Proof.

First, observe that we trivially have

β0\displaystyle\beta_{0} =arg⁡min⁡𝔼s​[C⋅(β⁡(W)−β0​(W))2]\displaystyle=\arg\min\mathbb{E}_{s}[C\cdot(\beta(W)-\beta_{0}(W))^{2}]
=arg⁡min⁡{𝔼s​[C⋅β​(W)2]+𝔼s​[C⋅β0​(W)2]−2​𝔼t​[C​β0​(W)​β​(W)]}\displaystyle=\arg\min\left\{\mathbb{E}_{s}[C\cdot\beta(W)^{2}]+\mathbb{E}_{s}[C\cdot\beta_{0}(W)^{2}]-2\mathbb{E}_{t}[C\beta_{0}(W)\beta(W)]\right\}
=arg⁡min⁡{𝔼s​[C⋅β​(W)2]−2​𝔼t​[C​β0​(W)​β​(W)]},\displaystyle=\arg\min\left\{\mathbb{E}_{s}[C\cdot\beta(W)^{2}]-2\mathbb{E}_{t}[C\beta_{0}(W)\beta(W)]\right\},

where the final inequality follows from noting that 𝔼s​[C⋅β0​(W)]\mathbb{E}_{s}[C\cdot\beta_{0}(W)] has no bearing on argument minimizer. Next, observe that we can equivalently write

𝔼s​[C⋅β0​(W)​β​(W)]=𝔼t​[β⁡(W)].\mathbb{E}_{s}[C\cdot\beta_{0}(W)\beta(W)]=\mathbb{E}_{t}[\beta(W)].

Putting these two observations together yields the desired result. ∎

In the setting of Algorithm 1, we can solve the empirical version of the loss on each fold to estimate β0\beta_{0}. In particular, we can let β^\widehat{\beta} be defined as

β^(−k):=arg⁡minβ∈ℱ​{K(K−1)​Ns​∑j∉ℐkCjs⋅β​(Wj)2−1Nt​∑i=1Ntβ⁡(Wit)},\widehat{\beta}^{(-k)}:=\arg\min_{\beta\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{\frac{K}{(K-1)N_{s}}\sum_{j\notin\mathcal{I}_{k}}C_{j}^{s}\cdot\beta(W_{j})^{2}-\frac{1}{N_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{t}}\beta(W_{i}^{t})\right\}, (10)

where ℱ\mathcal{F} denotes a chosen class of functions. In our applications (as discussed in Subsection E.3 of Appendix E) we choose to learn β0\beta_{0} over a class of feed-forward neural networks.

Appendix E Experiment Setup Details

E.1 Synthetic Dataset

Synthetic Data-Generating Process. We define the oracle nuisance functions:

π0​(X)\displaystyle\pi_{0}(X) :=P⁡(S=1∣X)=σ⁡(γ0+γX⊤​Φ​(X))\displaystyle:=P(S=1\mid X)=\sigma(\gamma_{0}+\gamma_{X}^{\top}\Phi(X)) (11)
μ0​(X)\displaystyle\mu_{0}(X) :=α0+αX⊤​Φ​(X)\displaystyle:=\alpha_{0}+\alpha_{X}^{\top}\Phi(X) (12)
ω0​(X)\displaystyle\omega_{0}(X) :=d​Ptd​Ps(X)=∏j=1dx(pt,jps,j)𝟏[Xj=1]\displaystyle:=\frac{dP_{t}}{dP_{s}}(X)=\prod_{j=1}^{d_{x}}\left(\frac{p_{t,j}}{p_{s,j}}\right)^{\mathbf{1}[X_{j}=1]} (13)
μ^​(X)\displaystyle\hat{\mu}(X) :=ρ⋅Y+1−ρ2⋅ϵ+b, for ​ϵ∼N⁡(0,σY2),b∈ℝ\displaystyle:=\rho\cdot Y+\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}\cdot\epsilon+b,\text{ for }\epsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^{2}_{Y}),b\in\mathbb{R} (14)

where Φ⁡(X)\Phi(X) represents polynomial feature expansion with interactions (degree 2), ps,jp_{s,j} and pt,jp_{t,j} are the Bernoulli parameters for feature jj in source and target domains respectively, ρ\rho controls the correlation between true and surrogate ratings, and bb represents surrogate bias.

We produce source and target datasets 𝒟s\mathcal{D}_{s} and 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} via the following procedure:

  1. 1.

    Sample domain membership: A∼Bernoulli​(pt)A\sim\text{Bernoulli}(p_{t}) where pt=ntns+ntp_{t}=\frac{n_{t}}{n_{s}+n_{t}}.

  2. 2.

    Sample categorical covariates: For each feature j∈{1,…,dx}j\in\{1,\ldots,d_{x}\}:

    • •

      If A=0A=0 (source): Xj∼2⋅Bernoulli​(ps,j)−1X_{j}\sim 2\cdot\text{Bernoulli}(p_{s,j})-1

    • •

      If A=1A=1 (target): Xj∼2⋅Bernoulli​(pt,j)−1X_{j}\sim 2\cdot\text{Bernoulli}(p_{t,j})-1

    This yields Xj∈{−1,1}X_{j}\in\{-1,1\} with different probabilities across domains.

  3. 3.

    Sample compliance status: For source domain only (A=0A=0):

    S∼Bernoulli​(π0​(X))S\sim\text{Bernoulli}(\pi_{0}(X))

    where compliance probability is determined by the scaled propensity model:

    π0​(X)=σ⁡(γ0β+β⋅γX⊤​Φ​(X))\pi_{0}(X)=\sigma\left(\frac{\gamma_{0}}{\beta}+\beta\cdot\gamma_{X}^{\top}\Phi(X)\right)

    and β∈[0.001,10]\beta\in[0.001,10] controls non-compliance rates (higher β\beta = more non-compliance).

    For target domain: S=0S=0 (no ratings available).

  4. 4.

    Generate true outcomes:

    Y=μ0​(X)+ϵY,ϵY∼N⁡(0,σy2)Y=\mu_{0}(X)+\epsilon_{Y},\quad\epsilon_{Y}\sim N(0,\sigma_{y}^{2})
  5. 5.

    Generate surrogate predictions:

    Y^=clip​(ρ⋅Y+1−ρ2⋅Z+b,ymin,ymax)\hat{Y}=\text{clip}(\rho\cdot Y+\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}\cdot Z+b,y_{\min},y_{\max})

    where Z∼N⁡(0,σY2)Z\sim N(0,\sigma_{Y}^{2}), ρ∈[0,1]\rho\in[0,1] controls correlation, and bb represents systematic bias.

  6. 6.

    Apply censoring: True ratings YY are only observed when S=1S=1 (compliant source raters).

We instantiate the above procedure with the following parameters dx=5d_{x}=5, σy=1.0\sigma_{y}=1.0, ps=(0.6,0.6,0.6,0.6,0.6)p_{s}=(0.6,0.6,0.6,0.6,0.6), pt=(0.3,0.5,0.1,0.4,0.3)p_{t}=(0.3,0.5,0.1,0.4,0.3). All synthetic experiments are run with Ns=2500N_{s}=2500 and Nt=2500N_{t}=2500.

E.2 Estimation Strategies

We now more formally describe the various estimators that we compare to our doubly-robust estimator.

  1. 1.

    Sample Average: The source mean estimator simply averages the samples coming from the source mean for which an outcome YY is observed, i.e. it produces an estimate θ^source\widehat{\theta}^{\text{source}} given by

    θ^source:=1∑j=1NsCj​∑j=1NsCj⋅Yj.\widehat{\theta}^{\text{source}}:=\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{N_{s}}C_{j}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{s}}C_{j}\cdot Y_{j}.

    Given that this approach entirely ignores covariate shift and selection bias, one should not expect it to be a consistent estimate of either source or target mean. We compute variance σ^source2\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{\text{source}} via

    σ^source2:=1∑j=1NsCj​∑j=1Ns(Cj​Yj−θ^source)2.\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{\text{source}}:=\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{N_{s}}C_{j}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{s}}(C_{j}Y_{j}-\widehat{\theta}^{\text{source}})^{2}.
  2. 2.

    Persona-Based: This approach opts to ignore source samples and instead averages the persona prediction Y^\widehat{Y} from the target distribution. That is, it produces and estimate θ^persona\widehat{\theta}^{\text{persona}} given by

    θ^persona:=1Nt​∑i=1NtY^i.\widehat{\theta}^{\text{persona}}:=\frac{1}{N_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{t}}\widehat{Y}_{i}.

    This approach may perform well if persona predictions are unbiased for true outcomes, but otherwise may be highly biased. The plug-in variance estimate we consider is

    σ^persona2:=1Nt​∑i=1Nt(Y^i−θ^persona)2.\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{\text{persona}}:=\frac{1}{N_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{t}}(\widehat{Y}_{i}-\widehat{\theta}^{\text{persona}})^{2}.
  3. 3.

    Persona Augmented Regression (PAR): The next approach uses the source data to estimate the outcome regression μ0​(w):=𝔼t​[Y∣W]≡𝔼s​[Y∣W]\mu_{0}(w):=\mathbb{E}_{t}[Y\mid W]\equiv\mathbb{E}_{s}[Y\mid W]. We use the entirety of the source data 𝒟s\mathcal{D}_{s} to learn a model μ^​(w,y^)\widehat{\mu}(w,\widehat{y}) predicting μ0\mu_{0} (we describe our particular nuisance estimation strategy below in Subsection E.3). Then, we compute our estimate θ^par\widehat{\theta}^{\text{par}} by

    θ^par:=1Nt​∑i=1Ntμ^​(Wi,Y^i).\widehat{\theta}^{\text{par}}:=\frac{1}{N_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{t}}\widehat{\mu}(W_{i},\widehat{Y}_{i}).

    We expect asymptotically normal confidence intervals constructed with this estimator to yield valid coverage only if we are able to estimate μ0\mu_{0} are fast, parametric rates. The corresponding plug-in variance estimate is

    σ^par2:=1Nt​∑i=1Nt(μ^​(Wi,Y^)−θ^par)2.\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{\text{par}}:=\frac{1}{N_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{t}}(\widehat{\mu}(W_{i},\widehat{Y})-\widehat{\theta}^{\text{par}})^{2}.
  4. 4.

    Inverse Propensity Weighted (IPW): Instead of estimating the regression function, one can instead estimate the reweighting coefficient α0​(w,c)=c​ω0​(w)π0​(w)\alpha_{0}(w,c)=c\frac{\omega_{0}(w)}{\pi_{0}(w)} and then use the estimated coefficient to re-weight labeled samples from the source distribution. To construct our IPW estimate, we again use KK-fold cross-fitting, constructing an estimate α^(−k)​(W,C)\widehat{\alpha}^{(-k)}(W,C) by using the data 𝒟s,kc\mathcal{D}_{s,k}^{c} and 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} on fold, as outlined in Algorithm 1. We discuss the specific nuisance estimator used below. Then, we construct our estimate as

    θ^ipw:=1Ns​∑k=1K∑j∈ℐkα^(−k)​(Wj,Cj)​Yj.\widehat{\theta}^{\text{ipw}}:=\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\widehat{\alpha}^{(-k)}(W_{j},C_{j})Y_{j}.

    Once again, we only expect intervals constructed around this estimator to yield valid coverage if estimation of α0\alpha_{0} occurs at parametric rates. The corresponding variance estimate is

    σ^ipw2:=1Ns​∑k=1K∑j∈ℐkα^(−k)​(Wj,Cj)2​{Yj−θ^i​p​w}2.\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{\text{ipw}}:=\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\widehat{\alpha}^{(-k)}(W_{j},C_{j})^{2}\left\{Y_{j}-\widehat{\theta}^{ipw}\right\}^{2}.
  5. 5.

    PPI++: We leverage the implementation of PPI++ found in Angelopoulos et al. (2023b) for computing both the estimator θ^PPI\widehat{\theta}^{\text{PPI}} itself and the sample variance σ^PPI2\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{\text{PPI}}, which we use for constructing confidence intervals.

  6. 6.

    RePPI: We implement the main algorithm in Ji et al. (2025) (Algorithm 1) for the point estimate θ^RePPI\widehat{\theta}^{\text{RePPI}} and leverage the variance estimate σRePPI2\sigma^{2}_{\text{RePPI}} outlined in Theorem 2 of their work. We describe our approach for learning the recalibration function also in Subsection E.3.

E.3 Nuisance Function Learning

We perform cross-fitting with K=5K=5 folds for DR approaches and IPW. We select the model for β0​(w):=ω0​(w)π0​(w)\beta_{0}(w):=\frac{\omega_{0}(w)}{\pi_{0}(w)} and for our outcome regression through hyperparameter tuning. These nuisance models are used to obtain estimates. We run this procedure separately for Synthetic, DICES, and PRISM, and retain the same set of hyperparameters for all settings of covariate shift and selection bias in each setting. For each setting, we sample from a grid containing the hyperparameters shown in Table 1. We found that weaker models (hidden dimension 32) better learned reweighting across different magnitudes of covariate shift, while deeper models (hidden dimension 64) better captured high non-compliance. For results reported in this paper, we opted for the weaker model to increase variance in the outcome regression and improve coverage across a range of covariate shift magnitudes.

E.4 Persona Simulation Framework

To simulate covariate shifts that may occur in real-world settings, we reference statistics reported by the U.S. Census Bureau (Guzman & Kollar, 2023) and the rater demographic distribution already present in DICES (Aroyo et al., 2023) which are reported in table 2.

E.4.1 LLM Usage

We use two LLMs (GPT-5 and GPT4o-Mini) to simulate human ratings for PRISM and four models to produce persona-based surrogate ratings for DICES (Claude-Sonnet-3.5, Claude-Haiku-3.5, GPT4o-Mini, and GPT-5). We use API calls for all LLMs with temperatures of 0.7 (for results reported in the main paper) and 0.9 for Anthropic models and 1 for OpenAI models. We use GPT-5 with reasoning set to “low.” Our exact system and user prompts are shown in Fig6,7,8.

E.5 Additional Empirical Results

In addition to the coverage plots reported in the main body of this paper, we include plots demonstrating how our method, DR (Riesz) achieves low bias (MAE) and higher coverage across a broad range of settings than existing methods and baselines.
